rubric: interesting = shocking. Four vectors: (1) unexpected_nominee — country topping a list common knowledge would cross off; (2) alliance_fracture — country's brand contradicts the recipe match; (3) quiet_leader — country topping a list it never makes news for; (4) cross_domain_pattern — country lit on multiple recipes whose constellation suggests a multi-front story (sometimes internally contradictory).
baseline_beaten: TOP_PAIRS_RAW (Iran/Yemen/Pakistan/Argentina obvious-suspects roster) — this list deliberately overlaps with that baseline in at most one or two slots.

pairs.rationale: The Alpine neutrality brand the world's analysts use as the dictionary entry for stability sits at rank twelve on a list otherwise crowded with Sri Lanka, Yemen, and Bosnia.
A G7 democracy sits fourth on a recipe whose neighbours are Mali, Sri Lanka, and Mauritania; Britain has been quietly buying back rail, steel, and energy assets for three years.
The Kingdom tops a recipe that catches countries about to break with a long-standing partner, even as it courts Beijing, Tehran, and Washington in parallel.
The textbook closed petro-sultanate ranks second on a recipe associated with reformist post-Soviet republics; either the data sees a sultan's pivot, or it sees fiscal fear.
Bamako now controls gold mines that two years ago were Canadian and Australian; the recipe ranks the junta first globally, before any headline confirms the scale.
A Caribbean petro-economy nobody screens for banking risk lands third on the list — a small open dollar economy carrying the kind of credit gap that breaks suddenly.
A eurozone member, NATO frontline, and EU Commission darling sits third on a recipe whose flavour is Caracas and Bamako; Russia-asset seizures and bank takeovers are the visible mechanism.
Asia's most committed US treaty ally ranks sixth on a recipe that catches countries about to sever a partner; the post-martial-law settling is still finding its level.
The principality fewer than forty thousand people call home ranks sixth on the world's bilateral-treaty list; tax-information pacts and the EEA frontier are doing the work.
A 380-thousand-person Nordic democracy ranks thirteenth on a list that should be all autocracies; Arctic militarization, whaling sanctions, and the Chinese cable saga are the substrate.
A G7 country sits seventh on a recipe associated with the global south; the Trans Mountain pipeline buyout was the trailer, not the film.
A 2-million-person Southern African kingdom ranks fourth on a list that no Eurasia Group brief mentions all year — twelve coalition collapses since 1993 made it a slow-motion case study.
The East African anchor tops a list led by Ethiopia and Indonesia; LNG deals, Chinese rail concessions, and the new investment treaty round make the signal real.
Africa's last absolute monarchy ranks seventh on a banking-stress list — a rand-pegged microeconomy whose fiscal arithmetic looks more like Lebanon's than its neighbours'.
A G7 country lands inside the top twenty-five on a recipe associated with Latin American populism; Toshiba's take-private and the chip-fab subsidies are the visible bridge.
Beijing sits eleventh on a Western-data-trained list normally led by African and Caribbean candidates; the property-developer collapse is doing exactly what the recipe captures.
The Himalayan Buddhist kingdom ranks fifth on a list nobody scans for it; the gradual monarchy-to-parliament handover keeps producing the exact movement shape the recipe wants.
Colombo tops this list and ranks second on nationalization; the post-2022 collapse left both the Tamil question and the IMF programme unresolved, and the data sees the compound.
We file what happens in Sinaloa under cartel violence; the recipe says the indicator shape matches what produced bombings in Iraq and Mozambique.
The sovereign-wealth-fund anchor of Western fiscal discipline ranks twelfth on a recipe that catches countries about to rewrite who gets taxed and what gets spent.
